strengths: The paper establishes a clear, elegant conceptual link between classical graphical model message passing on junction trees and distributional optimization / Estimation of Distribution Algorithms (EDAs).

The theoretical framework is well-developed, offering both a lower-bound expectation view on classical dynamic programming value functions and an alternate formulation based on maximum-entropy reinforcement learning / inference on graphs.

The experimental evaluation is clear and systematic, demonstrating consistent statistical sample efficiency and optimization gains over naive EDA across various synthetic landscapes and protein design benchmarks.
The ablation and case study on the contact distance threshold nicely illustrate the practical trade-off between model expressiveness (predictive accuracy) and decomposability (optimization ease).
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are narrow: DADO is only compared against a single decomposition-unaware autoregressive EDA. The paper would be significantly stronger if compared against other structured combinatorial optimization baselines (e.g., FDA, discrete Bayesian optimization with additive structures, or standard sequence RL methods like PPO/AWR).

In the protein experiments, the oracle objective function is explicitly trained to strictly enforce the junction tree decomposition. This creates an idealized setting where the ground-truth landscape matches the exact structural assumptions of DADO; it remains unclear how well DADO performs when optimizing an unconstrained, highly accurate sequence predictor (e.g., ESM-based models or standard CNN/Transformers) via an approximate decomposition.

The paper does not benchmark against exact or standard combinatorial solvers (e.g., junction tree dynamic programming, max-product belief propagation, or ILP). Given that classical message passing finds the exact global maximum of tree-decomposable functions, a comparison quantifying the trade-offs (runtime, memory, solution quality) between exact discrete optimization and distributional optimization is missing.

strengths: Principled and novel formulation: The paper establishes an elegant connection between classical junction tree message-passing and distributional optimization (EDAs / policy optimization), deriving a sample-efficient factorized update rule using distributional value functions.

Theoretical soundness and clarity: The paper provides clear mathematical derivations, including an informative connection between the message-passing dynamic programming lower bound and an alternate maximum-entropy policy optimization formulation in the appendix.

Clear writing and intuitive visualization: Figure 1 and Section 2 do an excellent job explaining how coordination via message-passing is achieved across overlapping factors compared to naive joint sampling or fully independent updates.

Thorough empirical analysis and ablations: The evaluation covers both synthetic landscapes with controlled epistatic interactions and multiple protein fitness datasets. The ablations on sample budget ($K$) and contact threshold ($t$), which controls the trade-off between decomposability and predictive fidelity, provide valuable insights.
weaknesses: Narrow baseline comparisons: The empirical evaluation almost exclusively compares DADO against a decomposition-unaware naive EDA. The paper would be significantly stronger with comparisons to other discrete optimization methods, such as standard discrete Bayesian optimization (e.g., tree-structured BO), genetic algorithms, or earlier decomposition-based evolutionary methods mentioned in the related work (such as the Factorized Distribution Algorithm).

Restricted objective function setup: In the protein experiments, the objective function $f(x)$ is explicitly parameterized to adhere strictly to the junction tree decomposition derived from contact maps. In many real-world applications, state-of-the-art property predictors are dense neural networks (e.g., transformers or protein language models) that do not possess exact tree factorizations. Evaluating how well DADO performs when optimizing an approximate decomposition against a dense, unconstrained ground-truth oracle would provide stronger validation of real-world utility.

Scalability with junction tree treewidth: When the underlying interaction graph is dense, junction tree treewidth can grow significantly, leading to large meta-variable node sizes. While the authors discuss this briefly and use MLPs for conditional factors, a more systematic analysis of computational scaling and memory requirements as treewidth grows would be beneficial.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and timely problem: improving the statistical and optimization efficiency of distributional optimization / Estimation of Distribution Algorithms (EDAs) in high-dimensional discrete scientific design spaces.
The methodology is conceptually elegant and well-formulated, neatly connecting graphical model message-passing / dynamic programming on junction trees with policy optimization and modern neural EDAs.

The derivation is clearly articulated, with intuitive parallels drawn between exact classical message passing and expected distributional value functions, supported by an alternative maximum-entropy formulation in the appendix.

The paper is well written, clearly organized, and includes thoughtful analyses, such as the ablation on sample budget K and the investigation of the trade-off between the contact threshold t (structural decomposition complexity) and predictive accuracy.
weaknesses: The experimental comparison is essentially restricted to a single baseline: an autoregressive, decomposition-unaware EDA. There are no comparisons against related structured EDAs (e.g., Factorized Distribution Algorithms or Bayesian Optimization Algorithms mentioned in Section 3), nor standard discrete optimization methods (e.g., simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, or exact/approximate message passing/max-product dynamic programming on the factor graph).

The evaluation setup for real protein benchmarks is somewhat synthetic/circular: the authors enforce the junction tree decomposition onto the predictive surrogate f(x) by training a decomposed neural network on assay data, and then optimize that exact decomposed network. While this provides a controlled testbed, it does not assess how well the method designs sequences under an unconstrained ground-truth oracle or standard complex fitness predictor.

The scalability with respect to junction tree treewidth (clique size) is not thoroughly characterized. For dense contact graphs or larger contact distance thresholds, the meta-variables can become large, which may impact the efficiency and parameterization of the conditional autoregressive models.

strengths: Principled and elegant formulation: The paper establishes a clear, rigorous bridge between classical dynamic programming/message-passing on junction trees and distributional optimization (EDAs/policy optimization), showing how intermediate value functions can provide localized credit assignment for factorized search distributions.

Well-motivated scientific application: Exploiting physical or structural locality (such as contact graphs from AlphaFold structures) to address combinatorial explosion in discrete sequence design is a natural and promising direction for AI-driven science.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and ablations: The authors validate the method across multiple synthetic setups (varying sequence length and alphabet size) and seven protein benchmark datasets, comparing against relevant baselines including naive EDA, FDA (which factorizes the search distribution without localized message passing), and PPO.

Thorough sensitivity analyses: The appendix provides extensive robustness studies exploring how varying contact distance thresholds, randomly perturbing decomposition edges, and distribution shifts (e.g., training on the bottom 50% of fitness values) impact predictive accuracy and downstream optimization.
weaknesses: Surrogate target functions are constrained to match the decomposition: In the protein experiments, the objective function being optimized is an MLP explicitly trained to strictly enforce the junction tree decomposition. While the authors show that this decomposed predictor achieves competitive holdout correlation compared to a dense neural network, optimizing an objective that is structurally guaranteed to factorize according to the tree is somewhat self-fulfilling. It remains unclear how well DADO would perform if an unconstrained black-box oracle (e.g., an ESM/transformer-based predictor or complex biophysical simulator) were optimized using an approximate decomposition tree for guidance.

Missing comparison to exact discrete optimization: For junction trees with small treewidth/node cardinality (such as cardinality $\le 5$ in the main text experiments), exact max-plus dynamic programming / junction tree algorithms can identify the global maximizer exactly and efficiently. Although the authors motivate distributional optimization via extensibility (e.g., sample diversity, Bayesian guidance, priors), the paper focuses on the pure EDA setting without priors or entropy bonuses. Benchmarking against classical exact solvers on these exact tree-decomposed functions would clarify when DO is practically competitive in terms of compute and solution quality.

Performance degradation on higher-treewidth graphs: As shown in Figures A4 and A5 for GB1, ynzC, and CreiLOV, DADO's performance degrades or fails to outperform FDA when node cardinality exceeds ~10–20 due to variance in Monte Carlo estimation of the distributional value functions. This poses a practical bottleneck for globular proteins or densely coupled systems unless contact thresholds are set aggressively low.

strengths: Principled and elegant formulation: The paper bridges classical junction-tree message-passing (max-plus dynamic programming) with modern estimation of distribution algorithms (EDAs) and policy optimization, providing a sound theoretical lower-bound connection and an insightful maximum-entropy RL derivation.

Statistical efficiency in discrete spaces: Decomposing the objective and factorizing the search distribution allows all $K$ samples to supervise low-dimensional conditional factors, addressing sample inefficiency in high-dimensional discrete optimization.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Experiments span multiple synthetic sequence lengths ($L \in \{25, 50, 100, 200, 400\}$) and alphabet sizes ($D \in \{20, 50, 100\}$), as well as seven real-world protein assay datasets using AlphaFold3 contact graphs.

Appropriate baselines and ablations: The comparison to FDA (which factorizes the search distribution but lacks message-passing value function weights) effectively isolates the specific utility of DADO's value function updates. Sensitivity analyses on graph mutations, contact thresholds, and runtime provide valuable insight.
High clarity and presentation quality: The manuscript is well-written, clearly motivated, and supported by informative diagrams and algorithmic descriptions.
weaknesses: Requirement of an explicitly decomposed surrogate: In real-world scientific design, black-box evaluators and modern deep learning predictors (e.g., ESM, large transformer-based property predictors) are rarely natively decomposed over low-treewidth junction trees. Forcing the surrogate model to strictly decompose into small cliques may limit model capacity compared to unrestricted state-of-the-art architectures.

Scalability bottlenecks on high-treewidth graphs: As shown in Appendix results for GB1, ynzC, and CreiLOV (where junction tree clique cardinalities exceed 10 to 20), DADO's advantage over baselines diminishes or reverses due to the high variance of Monte-Carlo value function estimates across large cliques.

Missing comparison against exact or combinatorial solvers: Because the objective $f(x)$ is explicitly constructed to decompose over a junction tree, classical exact dynamic programming (when clique states can be enumerated) or combinatorial solvers (e.g., Tree-Reweighted Max-Product, branch-and-bound, ILP) represent natural reference points for pure optimization, even if distributional optimization offers distinct advantages for sample diversity and Bayesian conditioning.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated conceptual framework: The paper provides an elegant extension of distributional optimization (estimation of distribution algorithms / policy optimization) to structured discrete spaces by leveraging junction tree decompositions and message passing.

Strong theoretical connections: The paper establishes clear connections between classical max-plus dynamic programming on junction trees and distributional value functions ($Q^\theta, V^\theta$), supported by an insightful alternative derivation via maximum entropy RL / PGMs in the appendix.

Promising empirical scaling: On synthetic tree-structured fitness landscapes, DADO convincingly demonstrates improved sample efficiency over standard EDA, FDA, and PPO baselines, with performance gaps growing significantly as sequence length ($L$) and alphabet size ($D$) scale.

Extensive analysis and reproducibility: The appendix contains comprehensive investigations, including sensitivity analyses on contact distance thresholds, random edge mutations, out-of-distribution training (bottom 50% data), and runtime comparisons across dimensions.
weaknesses: Surrogate evaluation is inherently tailored to the method: In the protein design experiments, the property predictive models $f(x)$ are explicitly parameterized as neural networks that strictly adhere to the junction tree decomposition. Optimizing a target function that was constructed specifically to satisfy the algorithm's factorization assumption leaves open how well the approach would perform when optimizing complex, non-factorized black-box oracles (e.g., full protein language models or physics-based energy functions) using an approximate junction tree.

Degradation on graphs with higher tree-width: As documented in the appendix (Figure A4 on GB1, ynzC, and CreiLOV), when junction tree node cardinalities exceed 5–10, DADO loses its advantage over FDA and standard baselines due to the high variance of Monte Carlo value function estimates, indicating practical constraints when applied to densely coupled systems.

Baselines are somewhat narrow: The empirical comparison focuses primarily on naive EDA, FDA (1999), and a simplified PPO variant. The paper would be strengthened by benchmarking against more contemporary discrete sequence design methods commonly used in ML-guided protein engineering (e.g., discrete GFlowNets, discrete diffusion/autoregressive guided generation, or Bayesian optimization with additive structures).
